summary: Creates the IANA registries for IAX, the Inter-Asterisk eXchange protocol, so that its numbers and codes are tracked in one place. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo makes official lists of the special numbers and names IAX uses, so people don't mix them up.

subtitle: Registries and code assignments for the IAX VoIP protocol

tldr.problem: IAX is a VoIP protocol that uses many numerical codes and types, and these need centralized registration to prevent conflicts and duplication.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5457 creates IANA registries for IAX's 15 namespaces, defining the valid ranges and providing initial assignments for frame types, control codes, media formats, and other identifiers.
tldr.outcome: Developers can now register new IAX values through IANA's expert review process instead of ad-hoc assignments.

today: RFC 5457 remains informational and provides the foundational registries for IAX. New values are still assigned through IANA's expert review process, allowing the protocol to grow while maintaining consistency.

sections.title: What IAX Is
sections.content:
IAX stands for Inter-Asterisk eXchange and is a protocol for handling multimedia communication over IP networks. It combines both control messages (to set up calls, hang up, etc.) and media (voice, video, or other data) in a single protocol. This is different from protocols like SIP, which separates signaling from media.

IAX was developed by the open source Asterisk PBX (Private Branch Exchange) project and is used primarily for Voice over IP (VoIP) calls. Its main advantages are compact encoding for low bandwidth use, simplified NAT (Network Address Translation) traversal by using a single UDP port, and the ability to carry new payload types without protocol changes.

Because IAX uses many different codes and types internally, IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) needs to maintain registries for all these values so developers can assign new ones in an organized way.
sections.plainLanguage: IAX is a way to make phone calls over the internet. It uses lots of special numbers for different things, so we need an official place to track them.

sections.title: IAX Namespaces
sections.content:
RFC 5457 establishes 15 registries for IAX's different namespaces. The most important ones are:

Frame Types (type 0x01 to 0x0A): These distinguish different kinds of data being sent. DTMF (0x01) carries dial tones, Voice (0x02) carries audio in various formats, Control (0x04) carries control messages like ringing or hangup, and IAX Control (0x06) carries protocol messages.

Control Frame Subclasses: These specify what a control frame means—like Hangup (0x01), Ringing (0x03), Answer (0x04), or Busy (0x05).

Information Elements: These are optional fields that can be included in IAX Control frames to carry information like calling number, called number, and authentication data.

Media Formats: These identify different audio and video codecs (compression formats) that can be sent over IAX.

Other registries track authentication methods, encryption methods, calling presentation settings, and cause codes for call failures.
sections.plainLanguage: IAX has 15 lists of special numbers. One list is for types of messages (voice, video, control). Others track codes for ring, answer, busy, what format a sound is in, and why a call failed.

sections.title: How to Register New Values
sections.content:
All registries in RFC 5457 use Expert Review as the registration procedure, as defined in RFC 5226. This means that new values are not automatically assigned but are reviewed by designated experts in the IAX protocol.

The RFC notes that new values should follow common-sense guidelines: they should not be specific to a single country, region, organization, or company. Instead, they should be well-defined and widely recognized. Documentation of new values is not mandated as RFCs; instead, a description and relevant security considerations are required.

Most registries have defined valid ranges (for example, Meta Command is 0x01 to 0x7F in hexadecimal). New assignments are only made within these ranges. The RFC provides initial assignments for each registry based on the IAX protocol definition in RFC 5456.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to add a new type of message or code to IAX, you ask an expert. They check that your idea is good and not just for one company.

sections.title: Important Registry Tables
sections.content:
The RFC provides detailed tables for the major registries. The Frame Types table lists all 10 frame types with their hex codes and descriptions. For example, Type 0x02 is Voice, carrying audio in various compression formats; Type 0x04 is Control with subclasses for status changes; and Type 0x06 is IAX Control with protocol-specific messages.

The Information Elements registry defines over 30 different IE types that can appear in IAX Control frames, including calling number, called number, calling name, authentication methods, encryption keys, and audio/video information.

The Media Formats registry maps numeric codes to specific audio codecs (G.711, GSM, etc.) and video codecs, allowing endpoints to negotiate which compression schemes to use for a call.

Other registries cover authentication methods (plaintext, MD5, RSA), encryption types, and cause codes for disconnection, which help explain why a call failed.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables say which number means voice, which means video, which means 'busy', and so on. They also list sound formats like phone quality audio or video compression.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC provides registries for security-related codes. The Authentication Methods registry includes plaintext password, MD5 challenge-response, and RSA signatures. The Encryption Methods registry defines which encryption algorithms can be used to secure IAX media and control channels.

The registries themselves do not impose security requirements, but they create a framework for tracking which authentication and encryption options are available. Implementers must use appropriate algorithms and follow best practices for key management and authentication.

The expert review process helps ensure that proposed new authentication or encryption methods meet security standards before being added to the registries.
sections.plainLanguage: The lists keep track of security recipes like MD5 and RSA that IAX can use. Experts check new security ideas before adding them.
